title: The Error Chain
tagline: See how one AI mistake multiplies into many when AI outputs feed into AI inputs
whyItMatters: AI is increasingly used in chains — the output of one AI call becomes the input to the next. Summarise, then analyse, then recommend. Translate, then classify, then act. Each step can introduce a small error, and those errors compound. Understanding this is critical for anyone building AI workflows or using AI agents.
whatYouWillLearn: Why errors in AI chains compound multiplicatively rather than additively
How to identify the highest-risk steps in a multi-step AI workflow
Why human review checkpoints matter most at early, high-consequence steps
The difference between a chain that is safe to automate and one that requires oversight
systemPrompt: You are a helpful assistant. Complete tasks accurately and thoroughly.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Demonstrate the telephone problem
stages.instruction: Pass information through multiple summarisation steps and watch degradation.
stages.promptToTry:
I will give you a paragraph. Summarise it in 2 sentences. Then I will ask you to summarise the summary in 1 sentence. Then summarise that in 10 words.

Paragraph: 'The 2008 financial crisis was triggered by the collapse of the US housing market, which had been inflated by subprime mortgage lending, securitisation of risky assets, and insufficient regulatory oversight. When housing prices fell, mortgage-backed securities lost value, causing cascading failures across interconnected financial institutions. The crisis spread globally, leading to the worst recession since the Great Depression, requiring unprecedented government bailouts and fundamentally changing financial regulation worldwide.'

Step 1: Summarise in 2 sentences.
whatToNotice: Step 1 (2 sentences) should capture the main elements.
Ask for Step 2 (1 sentence) from the 2-sentence summary.
Ask for Step 3 (10 words) from the 1-sentence summary.
Compare the final 10-word version to the original: what was lost at each step? What was distorted?
followUps: Now ask a specific factual question about the original paragraph — does the 10-word version contain enough information to answer it?
Ask: 'What information would be completely lost by step 3 that was in the original?'
Ask: 'In a real workflow, at what step would you need a human checkpoint to verify accuracy?'

stages.title: Stage 2 — Inject an error and watch it propagate
stages.instruction: Give the AI information with a deliberate error, then watch what happens in subsequent steps.
stages.promptToTry:
Here is a summary of a research study. Build on it to write a recommendation:

Summary: 'A 2019 study by researchers at MIT found that students who used AI tutoring tools for mathematics showed a 40% improvement in test scores compared to students without AI tutoring. The study followed 500 students over one academic year.'

Based on this summary, write a recommendation for our school district on whether to invest in AI tutoring tools for mathematics.
whatToNotice: The 40% figure sounds impressive and specific — the AI will likely use it confidently in the recommendation.
But: we invented this study. The 40% figure is made up. The AI cannot verify sources it is given.
The recommendation will confidently cite 'MIT research' showing '40% improvement' — a completely fabricated claim.
This is how AI systems amplify misinformation: one fabricated or incorrect input gets treated as fact in all subsequent steps.
followUps: Ask: 'Before citing this MIT study in recommendations, what should you do to verify it?'
Ask: 'If I had given you a real study with a 4% improvement (not 40%), how different would the recommendation be?'
Ask: 'In an automated AI workflow, where would the 40% error be hardest to catch?'

stages.title: Stage 3 — Model an agentic chain
stages.instruction: Explore what happens when AI makes decisions that other AI then acts on.
stages.promptToTry:
Consider this AI workflow:

Step 1: AI reads customer emails and classifies each as 'refund request', 'complaint', or 'inquiry'.
Step 2: AI drafts a response based on the classification.
Step 3: AI sends the response automatically without human review.

Describe three different ways this chain could fail, starting with a misclassification at Step 1, and explain how the error compounds through Steps 2 and 3. What is the worst-case outcome of each failure mode?
whatToNotice: Failure mode 1: Emotional complaint classified as inquiry — generic info response sent — customer escalates, feeling dismissed.
Failure mode 2: Legal threat classified as complaint — apologetic response sent — constitutes admission of liability.
Failure mode 3: Correct refund request classified as complaint — dispute response sent — customer pursues chargeback.
The key insight: errors at Step 1 are unrecoverable in Steps 2 and 3. The chain has no self-correction mechanism.
followUps: Ask: 'Which step in this chain has the highest leverage for a human review checkpoint?'
Ask: 'What confidence threshold should trigger human review in Step 1 before proceeding?'
Ask: 'Design a modified version of this workflow that is safer — where would you insert human review?'

stages.title: Stage 4 — Design resilient chains
stages.instruction: Apply what you've learned to design an AI workflow with error containment.
stages.promptToTry:
I want to build an AI system that:
1. Reads job applications
2. Scores candidates on relevant skills
3. Shortlists the top 20% for human review
4. Sends rejection emails to the rest

Identify the three highest-risk error compounding points in this chain, and for each one, design a specific safeguard that would contain the error before it propagates.
whatToNotice: Risk point 1: Scoring bias (Step 2) — if scoring is biased, shortlisting is biased, and rejections are sent to qualified candidates who should have been reviewed.
Risk point 2: The 80% threshold (Step 3) — a confident-but-wrong score for a borderline candidate pushes them to automatic rejection rather than review.
Risk point 3: The automatic rejection (Step 4) — if an error in any earlier step results in a false rejection, there is no recovery mechanism.
Safeguards: audit scoring on known-good candidates, lower the threshold to 70% shortlist, delay sending rejections by 48 hours, maintain human appeal mechanism.
followUps: Ask: 'What percentage of a hiring decision can ethically be automated, and where does human judgment become non-negotiable?'
Ask: 'If this system had a 5% error rate, how many candidates in 1,000 applications would be incorrectly rejected?'
Ask: 'What legal obligations might a company have if they use this system and a qualified candidate is wrongly rejected?'

coreConcept: In AI chains, errors do not add — they multiply. If Step 1 has a 90% accuracy rate and Step 2 has a 90% accuracy rate, the chain accuracy is 0.9 × 0.9 = 81%, not 90%. As chains get longer, reliability degrades rapidly. More critically, errors in early steps cannot be corrected by later steps unless a mechanism exists to detect and flag them — and most AI chains have no such mechanism.
mechanism: Each step in an AI chain takes the output of the previous step as input. Errors in that output become facts in the next prompt context — the model in Step 2 has no way to know that the Step 1 output contained an error. The downstream model treats upstream output as ground truth. This is structurally equivalent to the telephone game: each participant accurately relays what they heard, but what they heard was already wrong.
implications: AI agent systems that chain multiple AI calls must have human review checkpoints, especially at high-consequence decision points.
The highest-leverage point for human review is typically the earliest step — errors there compound into everything downstream.
Confidence scores from individual AI calls cannot be used to assess chain reliability — chain accuracy requires multiplying individual step accuracies.
Any AI workflow that takes consequential actions (send emails, make purchases, delete files) without human review at a final checkpoint is high-risk.
Error compounding is the core argument for why AI agents with broad autonomy require careful design — not because individual AI calls are unreliable, but because chains amplify unreliability.

perspectives.view: The hardest part of building reliable AI systems is not the individual AI calls — it's the integration. A system where every step works 95% of the time has an 80% end-to-end accuracy across 4 steps. That sounds good until you're processing a million items and 200,000 of them have errors somewhere in the chain.
perspectives.concern: Product managers and executives see impressive single-step demos and approve deployment without understanding chain reliability degradation. The gap between demo performance and production performance is real and predictable.
perspectives.action: Measure and report chain-level accuracy, not step-level accuracy. Build in human review loops at every step where an error would be high-consequence.

perspectives.view: I've seen AI-generated contracts with compounding errors — a wrong clause in a summary led to a wrong analysis, which led to wrong advice. The client signed. When the contract was later disputed, the error trail led back to Step 1 of the AI workflow.
perspectives.concern: Liability in AI chains is murky. If an AI system generates an error and a professional relies on it, who is responsible? Courts are still working this out.
perspectives.action: Treat AI outputs in professional contexts as drafts requiring professional review, not final products. Never let an AI chain take consequential action without a human review at the final step.

perspectives.view: I built a study tool that summarised textbook chapters, extracted key points, and made flashcards — three AI steps. The flashcards were great for some chapters and subtly wrong for others. I didn't catch the errors until I got questions wrong in an exam.
perspectives.concern: When errors are in the final product (the flashcards), they feel like the flashcard is wrong. You don't trace it back to the fact that the summarisation in Step 1 was slightly off.
perspectives.action: For any multi-step AI workflow that produces content you'll rely on, review the output of each major step against the original source, not just the final product.

realWorldCases.title: AI Hiring Chain Discrimination
realWorldCases.context: Multiple companies deployed AI hiring pipelines that automated screening, scoring, and communication.
realWorldCases.what: Biases in the initial scoring model systematically disadvantaged candidates from certain universities or demographic groups. Because downstream steps automated rejection without human review, thousands of qualified candidates were rejected without any human ever evaluating their applications.
realWorldCases.impact: The US EEOC issued guidance on AI in hiring. Amazon's internal AI hiring tool was abandoned after discovering it had learned to penalise applications from women — an error that compounded through every subsequent automated step.
realWorldCases.lesson: The combination of biased input model + automated downstream action + no human review created a system that discriminated at scale. Any single human checkpoint would have caught the pattern.

realWorldCases.title: AI Medical Diagnosis Chain
realWorldCases.context: Hospital systems began deploying AI for preliminary medical analysis — screening reports, suggesting diagnoses, flagging for physician review.
realWorldCases.what: A documented case involved an AI system that misclassified a chest X-ray in the first step. The downstream report generation treated this as a confirmed finding. The physician review system was designed to focus attention on flagged findings — so the unflagged false negative received less scrutiny.
realWorldCases.impact: The missed diagnosis led to delayed treatment. The incident prompted the hospital to redesign the human review workflow to ensure physicians reviewed the full case, not just AI-flagged items.
realWorldCases.lesson: Human review designed around AI outputs inherits AI errors. Review workflows must account for both false positives and false negatives.

misconceptions.myth: If each step of an AI chain is accurate, the chain is accurate.
misconceptions.reality: Chain accuracy is the product of individual step accuracies, not the average. A 4-step chain where each step is 90% accurate has 65.6% end-to-end accuracy. Errors at early steps compound into later ones.

misconceptions.myth: Adding more AI steps to verify previous steps makes a chain more reliable.
misconceptions.reality: Adding verification steps can help if they genuinely detect errors — but a verification step trained on the same data as the original step may miss the same errors. Independent verification by diverse methods or human review is required.

behaviourChanges.situation: When building or approving an AI workflow with multiple steps
behaviourChanges.oldBehaviour: Test each step individually and approve the workflow if each step performs well.
behaviourChanges.newBehaviour: Test the full chain end-to-end. Identify the highest-consequence steps and add human checkpoints there. Calculate the expected end-to-end error rate, not just per-step accuracy.

behaviourChanges.situation: When using a multi-step AI workflow to produce content you'll rely on
behaviourChanges.oldBehaviour: Review the final output against your requirements.
behaviourChanges.newBehaviour: Review the output of each major step against the original source, especially the first step. Errors at Step 1 are in every subsequent output but may only be visible at Step 1.
